newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: IMF conditionally agrees to resume loan programme.
newsitem.headline: IMF conditionally agrees to resume loan programme.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has decided to resume a $120 million loan programme to Cambodia if the government takes concrete action to improve its forestry policies, Cambodian officials said on Friday.
The officials said the decision reflected recognition by the IMF that Cambodia had made some improvements in its forestry policies since last November.
The fund had cancelled a $20 million loan installment then on concerns about heavy logging and accounting procedures for forestry revenues.

"The IMF mission team recognises that Cambodia has made some progress since their last visit," said Secretary of State for Finance Sun Chanthol, adding, "Cambodia is doing the best it can with limited resources."

Michael Kuhn, assistant director of the IMF's Central Asia Department, confirmed that $40 million, representing the third disbursement of a three-year, $120 million programme, would be made available in two installments on certain conditions.
He declined to provide details of the conditions.
Sun Chanthol said that the government had agreed late Wednesday to two conditions on forestry and three general conditions, including the adoption of a sub-decree to Cambodia's investment law.
If Cambodia meets those criteria by May, it would receive $20 million soon after, Sun Chanthol said.
"All the conditions will be met by the end of May. There is nothing drastic that we cannot do," he said.

He would not provide further details on any of the criteria until he had briefed co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, but officials familiar with the past 10 days of discussions between the government and IMF said reform of Cambodia's bloated civil service was involved.

Analysts agreed that technically, Cambodia was fully capable of meeting the IMF's conditions, but that government commitment to the principles of sustainable forestry and transparency in government finances would be harder to achieve.
"The problem is political will," said one Cambodian analyst.
The analysts noted that despite enforcement of a December 31 ban on log exports, the government has admitted illegal logging continues, even in the national parks.
Cambodia lost 1.4 million hectares (3.5 million acres) of forest between 1973 and 1993, with logging expanding each year.
The British environmental group Global Witness, long a critic of Cambodia's forestry policies, expressed cautious optimism about the IMF's decision.
"We hope the IMF's conditions reinforce the existing export legislation," said a statement from the group.
As for the final installment of the loan programme, Sun Chanthol said the last $20 million payment would be contingent upon two or three additional conditions.
The government derives about 40 percent of its budget from foreign aid, and analysts say many agencies, including the World Bank and Asian Development Bank take their lead from the IMF.
